clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive defect of carnitine palmitoyltransferase 2 on the matrix face of the inner mitochondrial membrane, which regenerates long-chain acyl-CoA from acylcarnitine after translocase-mediated import, the counterpart to carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1.

Three phenotypes span a severity spectrum: a lethal neonatal form with multisystem failure, cystic dysplastic kidneys, cerebral malformation, cardiomyopathy and hepatomegaly; a severe infantile hepatocardiomuscular form; and the common myopathic form of adolescence and adulthood.
The late-onset myopathic form is the commonest inherited cause of recurrent rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria, classically provoked by prolonged exercise, fasting, cold or fever.
In the myopathic form muscle strength and creatine kinase are typically normal between attacks.
The common thermolabile myopathic variant is p.Ser113Leu, which helps explain the characteristic fever- and cold-related triggers.

The acylcarnitine profile shows raised long-chain species (C16, C18:1, C18:2) that are indistinguishable from carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase deficiency, so enzyme or molecular testing is needed to separate the two.
Severe myoglobinuria can precipitate acute kidney injury.
Management comprises fasting avoidance, long-chain-fat restriction with medium-chain triglyceride, generous carbohydrate around exertion, and prompt glucose during illness.
reference.pathophysiology: After carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 forms long-chain acylcarnitine and the carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase shuttles it across the inner mitochondrial membrane, carnitine palmitoyltransferase 2 on the matrix side reconverts acylcarnitine back to acyl-CoA plus free carnitine so that beta-oxidation can proceed. Loss of this enzyme therefore blocks long-chain fatty-acid oxidation, and the clinical severity tracks residual activity. Near-absent activity produces the neonatal lethal or severe infantile multisystem disease, whereas the partially active, thermolabile variants typical of the myopathic form leave enough function for daily life but fail under the metabolic demand of prolonged exercise, fasting, cold or fever, when muscle energy supply collapses and toxic long-chain acylcarnitines accumulate and destabilise the sarcolemma, triggering rhabdomyolysis. The developmental malformations of the neonatal form are attributed to profound fatty-acid-oxidation failure during organogenesis.
additionalDifferentials: Carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase deficiency, which gives an identical acylcarnitine pattern
Long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase and trifunctional protein deficiency
McArdle disease and other glycogenoses causing exertional rhabdomyolysis
Muscular dystrophies presenting with exertional myalgia
Other causes of neonatal multiorgan failure with cystic renal dysplasia
additionalInvestigations: Plasma acylcarnitine profile showing elevated long-chain species
Molecular testing of CPT2, including the common p.Ser113Leu variant
Carnitine palmitoyltransferase 2 enzyme activity in muscle, fibroblasts or leucocytes
Creatine kinase and urine myoglobin during acute attacks
Echocardiography and electrocardiography in the infantile and neonatal forms
Neonatal cerebral and renal imaging in the severe form
redFlags: Pigmenturia with markedly raised creatine kinase and threatened acute kidney injury
Neonatal multiorgan failure with cystic dysplastic kidneys and dysmorphism
Cardiomyopathy or arrhythmia in the infantile form
reference.prognosis: The myopathic form is compatible with a normal lifespan when triggers are avoided, although rhabdomyolysis recurs; the infantile form carries high morbidity and the neonatal form is usually fatal.
pitfalls: Attributing recurrent exertional rhabdomyolysis to deconditioning or to a statin effect
Assuming that a normal creatine kinase between episodes excludes the diagnosis
Attempting to distinguish it from translocase deficiency on the acylcarnitine profile alone
Administering long-chain lipids during an acute crisis
Missing the associated renal and cerebral malformations in the neonatal presentation
references: Fatty acid oxidation disorder management consensus guidelines
management: Prevent attacks by avoiding recognised triggers of prolonged exercise, fasting, cold and fever, with carbohydrate loading before sustained exertion
Adopt a low-long-chain-fat diet with medium-chain triglyceride supplementation
Treat acute rhabdomyolysis with intravenous glucose, generous hydration and measures to protect renal function from myoglobinuria
Support cardiac, hepatic and metabolic function in the severe infantile and neonatal forms
Monitor creatine kinase, urinary myoglobin and renal function during attacks
Manage within a specialist metabolic team
Offer CPT2 genetic testing, including the common thermolabile variant, with counselling and family screening, given autosomal recessive inheritance
